Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 12:37: The Righteous One [Tzaddik/Yesod] is called faithful, for it is explained in the Tikkunim (34b) and in Ra'aya Meheimna (parashat Pinchas 229a) that in the Righteous One is the secret of "amen," whose numerical value is ninety-one, equal to YaHDoNHY [YHVH+Adonai combined]; and in the Righteous One is this Name, for he is called "kol" ["all"] — "in heaven and on earth" — bound in heaven and on earth, as explained in the Tikkunim (29a). And regarding "amen," it is explained at the end of parashat Vayelech (285b) that it is an acronym for "El Melech Ne'eman" ["God, faithful King"] — thus "faithful" is in the Righteous One. It follows that wherever "amen" is found, as explained in parashat Vayelech — see there — "faithful" is found. And further they explained in Tractate Shabbat (104a) regarding the letter "nun" — bent, "faithful [ne'eman] bent"; upright, "faithful upright."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 12:38: It follows in general that "faithful" is found in all four letters of the Name, and this is the essence of faith; therefore the first mention of the word "emunah" found in the Torah is found with the Name YHVH, as it says (Genesis 15:6), "and he believed in YHVH," etc., and likewise afterward (Exodus 14:31), "and they believed in YHVH." You already know what the Rashbi, peace be upon him, said (Tikkunei Zohar 92b), that in this Name is the essence of Israel's faith — and we quoted his words in the Gate of Fear, chapter 1 — where he said: and therefore Israel's faith is placed in these four letters, in all the [other] names he places designations corresponding to this Name. And it is explained there that the Cause of causes unifies the four letters of YHVH; it follows that the faithful one binds himself to His great Name and to the Cause of causes — happy is he.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 12:39: Now, regarding the matter of joy, we have already explained that joy comes from trust and faith — for the servant who trusts in his master and believes he will pay him doubled and redoubled reward for his labor, serves with joy, and he is joyful in whatever is decreed upon him, and he thus bears everything, like the sick person who eats bitter medicines for the sake of healing — and one who bears things patiently is free from the worries of the world.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 12:40: There is a further benefit in joy, as with the two men whom Elijah said were destined for the World to Come, because they were joyful people, and when they saw a sad person they would gladden him, and when they saw two quarreling with one another, they would speak jesting words to them until they made peace between them (Ta'anit 22a). And so regarding halachic study, one should begin with jesting words to open the heart to study joyfully (Shabbat 30b) — though not the joy of scoffers or misers, but rather the matter of a commandment, which gladdens the heart, as it is written (Psalms 19:9), "the precepts of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart" — and all this is the joy of a commandment.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 12:41: On the attribute of joy depends the positive commandment that a person justify God's judgment over all that befalls him, as it is said (Deuteronomy 8:5), "and you shall know in your heart, that as a man disciplines his son, so the Lord your God disciplines you." And if, after a person has repented, his affairs do not go as well as before, then it is a positive commandment that he think in his heart that his affairs have turned to evil for his own good — for before he repented, the Holy One, blessed be He, was paying him the reward of a commandment in order to remove him from the World to Come. All this depends on the attribute of joy — one who is joyful with his portion that God, blessed be He, apportioned to him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 12:42: The way a person should rejoice in his portion is that he rejoice at evil just as at good, and bear it with joy — for one who bears things patiently is free from the worries of the world, for he who bears patiently is content with the little he has, saying, it is enough for me what the Creator, blessed be He, decrees for me.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 12:43: Now look and see that joy encompasses everything — for whoever worries about this world has no rest all his days, for he is always scheming to gain wealth, and is never content with what God, blessed be He, has apportioned him; therefore whoever is joyful with his portion is rich even if he is poor, for he rejoices in the Name, since He is his inheritance, as it is written (Lamentations 3:24), "the Lord is my portion, says my soul," and it is written (Psalms 16:5), "the Lord is the portion of my inheritance and my cup," etc., and it is said (ibid. 105:3), "let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice" — and this attribute belongs only to the souls of the righteous, who are in complete pleasantness in their service and in great joy in their abstinence, as it is said (ibid. 32:11), "be glad in the Lord and rejoice, O righteous, and shout for joy, all who are upright in heart," and it is said (ibid. 97:11), "light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 12:44: Therefore, everyone should place his joy upon the Torah, and at the time he performs the commandments, he should rejoice in his heart that he has merited to be a servant to the Supernal King, before whom the beings of the higher realm bow. So David said (Psalms 119:162), "I rejoice at Your word, like one who finds great spoil." And whoever performs a commandment with joy has a reward a thousand times greater than one who is merely commanded.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 12:45: Abraham and David were engaged in Torah all day, and glorified and praised with songs and praises of the Holy One, blessed be He, raising their voices in joy, and then all their limbs were saved with their goodly pleasantness, and the holy spirit was sent within them, and their hearts rejoiced and were filled with love of the Holy One, blessed be He, and their souls were bound in exultation, and secrets and novel insights of exaltedness were revealed to them — because they feared the Name and were upright, pleasantness entered within them. This is what Solomon the king, peace be upon him, said (Song of Songs 5:6), "my soul went out at His word," and "and my kidneys shall exult when Your lips speak upright things" (Proverbs 23:16). And so David said (Psalms 104:1), "bless the Lord, O my soul" — because the soul is what ascends and rises, and just as it knows the matter of its own secret, then it loves the Creator and treasures His commandments, and when the soul reaches its exalted place, to which it is akin, it then unifies Him in its innermost being and delights in His chambers, and at every moment and instant desires His love and remembers Him at night upon its couch — then the Name, blessed be He, sends within it the desire for joy, in the manner it is said (Isaiah 61:10), "I will greatly rejoice in the Lord, my soul shall exult in my God" — and happy is the soul that merits to see this joy. And the Shechinah rests only through joy, and none of the prophets prophesied whenever they wished, but only when they composed their minds and sat joyful and good-hearted and secluded themselves — for prophecy rests neither through sadness nor through laziness but through joy; therefore the sons of the prophets had before them a tambourine, a flute, and a harp, and sought prophecy, as it is written (II Kings 3:15), "and it came to pass, when the minstrel played, that the hand of the Lord came upon him."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 12:46: Love is the beauty of the soul, which is beautified with the beauty of joy, rejoicing in its God, and clings to the splendor of the fear of the Name, to cling to the preciousness of His majesty, and the light of its longing for its Former mingles with the love of its desire, the passion of supernal longing, to be crowned with the crown of beauty of pure and clean thoughts, and it moans out of the greatness of the joy of its delight for its Beloved, the Supernal Beloved, and is bound with the bonds of affection, and seeks and searches after the ranks, to shine with the light of life. And at the time it exalts and magnifies itself to know the holiness of its Former, and clings in its faithfulness to its Creator, it then spreads out in gladness and exultation and expands in joy, and at that moment it is sanctified with the holiness of the Holy of Holies, and then it is beloved and finds favor before the King of Kings, and at that time it is established, beautified, and adorned with the glory of the pride of the might and splendor of the beauty of love, and then the Supernal One treasures it, to make its splendor shine, to bring it into chambers of radiance and to bind it in the bond of life. May the Merciful One make us among those who serve Him and rejoice in Him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 12:47: This chapter I have compiled from Chovot HaLevavot in the Gate of Trust, and from the book Beit Middot found among us in manuscript, and what I have added to it according to what the Name has graced me — as the discerning reader will see what is an addition. It is upon us to entreat the favor of God, that He guide us in the path of His commandments and His Torah, to be among those who love His Name — Amen, and so may it be His will.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 12:48: With this the chapter and the Gate are concluded:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:1: Before we enter into the explanation of the attributes of repentance, we must explain how many exhortations there are for it, and when a person reads these words from the sayings of our sages, of blessed memory, his heart will be aroused to repent.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:2: Because the Holy One, blessed be He, is abundant in kindness, and created the world through His kindness, as a free gift without any necessity — because His attribute is to do good, and He wished to do good to the existing things and that they recognize His greatness, for this is the essential purpose of the creation of the world, "in order that they might know Him," as explained in Ra'aya Meheimna (parashat Bo el Par'oh 42b) — and the creation of the whole world was created only for the sake of Israel, who are called "the beginning [reishit]"; this is [why the Torah begins] "Bereishit [in the beginning] God created" — for the sake of Israel, who are called "reishit," as it is said (Jeremiah 2:3), "Israel is holy to the Lord, the first-fruits [reishit] of His increase."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:3: The Holy One, blessed be He, in His wisdom saw the necessity of creating souls through the good inclination and the evil inclination, so that they receive good reward according to their deeds and according to judgment — for if He were to create without the evil inclination, it would be an angel, and for this the angels were already created. There is a further reason, explained in the Zohar (parashat Bereishit 23a), that since man was created with the evil inclination, it is impossible that he not sin — for few indeed, according to the view of our sages, of blessed memory, died only through the serpent's scheming, in whom no sin was found (Shabbat 55b) — and for this reason repentance preceded the creation of the world, as explained in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (ch. 3), that seven things preceded the world, and one of them is repentance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:4: So too they said in the Zohar (parashat Acharei Mot 69): we have learned, at the time the Holy One, blessed be He, created the world and wished to create man, He took counsel with the Torah; she said before Him, You seek to create this man — he is destined to sin before You, he is destined to be angry before You; if You will treat him according to his deeds, this world cannot stand before You, how much less that man. He said to them, is it then for nothing that I am called "a God merciful, gracious, and slow to anger"? And before the Holy One, blessed be He, created the world, He created repentance. He said to Repentance, I wish to create man in the world, on condition that when they return to You from their sins, You shall be ready to forgive their sins and atone for them; and at every single moment, repentance is ready for human beings, and when human beings return from their sins, this repentance returns to the Holy One, blessed be He, and atones for all, and the judgments are subdued and all are sweetened, and man is purified from his sin. When is man purified from his sin? At the moment he enters into this repentance properly. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:5: Now, the matter of repentance, the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded us regarding it in His holy Torah through Moses our teacher, peace be upon him (Numbers 5:6), "a man or a woman who commits any sin that men commit... shall confess their sin which they have done, and shall make restitution for his guilt in its full amount." And it says (Deuteronomy 4:30), "when you are in distress, and all these things have come upon you... you shall return to the Lord your God and listen to His voice, for the Lord your God is a merciful God, He will not fail you nor destroy you." And in parashat Atem Nitzavim it says (ibid. 30:1), "and it shall come to pass, when all these things come upon you, the blessing and the curse," etc., "and you shall take it to your heart," etc., "and shall return to the Lord your God and listen to His voice," and it says afterward (ibid. 30:8), "and you shall return and listen to the voice of the Lord," and it returns and says, "when you return to the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:6: The Ramban, peace be upon him, wrote in his commentary on the Torah (parashat Nitzavim, p. 121) that even the verse "for this commandment" (ibid. 30:11), if it speaks of the Torah, it should have said "the entire commandment which I command you today," etc. And although this is not really a difficulty, since he explained all these verses as referring to the Torah, which is called "this Torah" (Numbers 19:14) — nevertheless, the Torah has seventy facets, and it is possible to reconcile it also with repentance, since the attribute of "Zot" ["this"] is also called repentance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:7: In my opinion, the verse may be reconciled: "for the matter is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, to do it" — that is, "in your mouth" refers to the verbal confession one must make; "and in your heart" refers to the acceptance of repentance in one's heart and the abandonment of the sin; "to do it" — if he stole, that he return the stolen goods, and the like.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:8: Further, our holy Torah alerted us to the exhortation of repentance, in parashat Mishpatim, in these verses (Exodus 21:7): "and if a man sells his daughter as a maidservant, she shall not go out," etc., "if she is displeasing in the eyes of her master." And it is explained in the Zohar (parashat Mishpatim, end of p. 96), in these words: the Torah, which gives counsel to the whole world, saw this and warned the people of the world, saying: see how much the Holy One, blessed be He, has compassion upon you — a precious pearl He had, He sold it to you for free, that you might be enslaved by it in this world. "And if a man sells his daughter" — this is the Holy One, blessed be He; "his daughter" — this is the holy soul; "as a maidservant" — that the maidservant be enslaved among you in this world, at your entreaty — at the time the moment comes for it to depart the world, "she shall not go out" like the [ordinary] slaves go out — that it should not go out soiled, should not go out defiled with sins, but rather go out free, clear and clean, so that its Master rejoices in it and is praised through it, and gives it good reward in the purities of the Garden of Eden, as it is said (Isaiah 58:11), "and satisfy your soul in drought" — surely, when it goes out clean and clear as is fitting. But "if it is displeasing in the eyes of its master" — soiled with the filth of sins, and does not appear before Him as is fitting — woe to that body from which that soul is lost forever, because when souls ascend clear and go out clean from this world, each and every soul enters into the King's book of records, and all of them by name, and it says, this is the soul of so-and-so, destined to belong to that body it left — then it is written "lo ye'adah" ["designated for him"] with a vav [implying certainty]. But when it comes out displeasing in the eyes of its master, having been defiled with sins and the filth of transgressions, then it is written "lo yo'adah" with an aleph [implying negation, "not designated"], and that body is lost to it, and it will not be assigned to it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:9: Except if the master desires the repentance of the body — then it is written "veh-hefdah" ["then he shall let it be redeemed"], as it is said (Job 33:28), "He redeems his soul from passing into the pit." "Veh-hefdah" — this refers to a person whose intent is to redeem it and return in repentance; and in two respects the Holy One, blessed be He, says "veh-hefdah" — through repentance: after he has returned in repentance, He redeems it from the path of Gehinnom.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:10: "To a foreign people he shall have no power to sell her" — who is "a foreign people"? This poor soul, when it leaves the world, and a person has strayed from his way with it, it wishes to ascend above among the holy camps, for the holy camps stand upon that path of the Garden of Eden, and the foreign camps stand upon that path of Gehinnom. If the soul is meritorious, how many holy camps prepare themselves to join with it and bring it into the Garden of Eden; if it is not meritorious, how many foreign camps prepare themselves on the path of Gehinnom, and these are camps of destroying angels ready to take vengeance upon it. The verse comes and warns, "to a foreign people he shall have no power to sell her" — these being destroying angels. "Since he has dealt deceitfully with her" — since it is the guarded charge of the Holy One, blessed be He, He guards it so that no foreign people rule over it, with that spread of protection over it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:11: "But if he betroths her to his son" — come and see how much a person must be careful not to stray from his ways in this world, for if a person merits in this world and guards his soul properly, this is a person the Holy One, blessed be He, desires, and boasts of him every day among His retinue, and says: see the holy son I have in that world, such and such he does, such and such are his deeds properly ordered. And when this soul leaves this world meritorious, clean, and clear, the Holy One, blessed be He, illumines it with several lights, and every day He calls out over it, this is the soul of so-and-so, My son — and this is what is written, "but if he betroths her to his son." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:12: This is an exhortation to a person along the path of reason — that since the soul is the daughter of the King of Kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, and the Holy One, blessed be He, entrusted it to man in this world against its will, as explained there, and man makes use of the soul for the needs of the body — and its descent into this world was only for the rectification of Torah and commandments, as is known — this is what is said, a precious pearl He had, He sold it to you for free, that you might be enslaved by it in this world; at the very least, what the Holy One, blessed be He, asked of us is not to soil His deposit through the filth of transgressions.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:13: And if it is soiled, that he redeem it immediately from the hands of the kelipot, as it is said, "veh-hefdah" — and through this he will not allow a foreign people to rule over it in Gehinnom. This is a second exhortation to a person — that it is fitting that he have compassion on the clean pearl the Creator gave him, that it is not fitting for him to soil it, so that it need go to Gehinnom to be refined — this being what they said in Tractate Shabbat (152b) on the verse (Ecclesiastes 12:7), "and the spirit shall return to God" — give it back to Him as He gave it to you — the intent being to exclude the soiling of sins, but not that he should give it back to Him without the adornments of Torah and commandments, for if it returns as it came, what has it gained by coming into the world?
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:14: A further, third exhortation — it is fitting that one be aroused to return in repentance when he considers that the Shechinah is exiled because of us, as it is written (Isaiah 50:1), "and because of your transgressions your mother was sent away" — and her release from exile depends on our repentance; why should not each and every one be aroused to repentance, to lighten the yoke of exile from upon her, and to illuminate what has been blemished in her, as we elaborated at length in the Gate of Fear, on how we cause blemish to her and prolong the exile.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:15: This aspect is explained in the Tikkunim (22a), in these words: woe to human beings, for whom the Holy One, blessed be He, is bound in exile with them, and the Shechinah is bound with them, and of it is said, "none imprisoned can free himself from prison" — and her redemption, which is repentance, the Supernal Mother, depends on their hands, for she has fifty gates of freedom with her, corresponding to the fifty times the Exodus from Egypt is mentioned in the Torah — this is "and he turned this way and that" ["koh va-koh"] — through these fifty letters by which she is unified every day, twice, in the Shema, which contain twenty-five and twenty-five letters. "And he saw that there was no man" — that she is aroused for their sake, and she watches from the windows, of which it is said (Malachi 1:9), "beseech now the favor of God, that He be gracious to us" — for the One of whom it is said (Numbers 12:13), "O God, please heal her now," whose remedy is in His own hand — for it is stretched out to receive the penitent — "and he saw that there was no man."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:16: She looks forth through the window and wails, with a broken cry that is a wail, of which it is said (Genesis 8:6), "and Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made" — and this is Yom Kippur, for Noah's ark is the Supernal Mother, and her window is the central column, in which is light, and "Torah is light," and this is the hidden light. "And he turned this way and that" — peering through the crevices — these are the Ten Days of Repentance — "and he saw that there was no man."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:17: Further, she watches from the windows — these being the windows of the synagogue, for the Father [Abba] and His children are imprisoned in the synagogue, and every day she watches over them and gives them sustenance. "And he turned this way and that" — if there is anyone aroused to repentance, to break their prison house, this being what is written (Isaiah 49:9), "saying to the prisoners, go out; to those who are in darkness, reveal yourselves" — "and he turned this way and that, and he saw that there was no man" — but rather each man turned to his own way, occupied with their own affairs, in their own paths, each man to his gain from his own quarter, in the gain of this world, to inherit this world, and they are not from the side of those of whom it is said (Exodus 18:21), "men of valor, fearing God, men of truth, hating unjust gain" — but rather, "and he saw that there was no man," but rather they all cry out in prayers on Yom Kippur like dogs, "give, give" us sustenance and forgiveness and atonement and "inscribe us for life," and they are brazen of soul like dogs, like the idol-worshiping nations of the world who cry out to Him with no shame at all, for there is no one to call them to repentance, that the Holy One, blessed be He, restore the Shechinah to Himself in the manner He restores it to them — and they resemble dogs, of whom it is said (Psalms 106:35), "and they mingled with the nations and learned their deeds" — and they are the mixed multitude [erev rav], for all the kindness they perform, they perform for themselves. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:18: Here it is explicitly stated how fitting it is that we be aroused to repentance out of love for the Shechinah, to raise her up from exile — not in order to receive reward, and that we not resemble the mixed multitude or the idol-worshiping gentiles mentioned in this passage.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:19: In the manner the Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in this passage — that it is a brazen-faced person who comes on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur to say "inscribe us for life" and to ask for forgiveness and atonement without an arousal of repentance — in this same manner, every single day, too, when we make several requests in our prayer, which are the thirteen middle blessings, the Holy One, blessed be He, might say, since you come to ask that I do this and that for you, what is the repentance you have made? — although we ask, "return us, our Father, to Your Torah," and "forgive us."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:20: So too we find in Vayikra Rabbah, parashat "This shall be the law of the metzora" (16:4): we find in the Torah, in the Prophets, and in the Writings, that He desires no praise from the wicked. In the Torah, as it is written (Leviticus 13:45), "and he shall cover his upper lip and cry, impure, impure." In the Prophets, as it is written (II Kings 8:5), "and it came to pass, as he was recounting to the king how he had revived the dead," etc., "this is the woman, and this is her son" — were they then standing behind the door [waiting for this cue]? The rabbis say: even if they were at the end of the world, the Holy One, blessed be He, brought them near, so that that wicked one [Gehazi] would not recount the wonders of the Holy One, blessed be He. In the Writings, as it is written (Psalms 50:16), "but to the wicked, God says, what right have you to declare My statutes, that you should take My covenant in your mouth?" — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:21: Therefore one must return in repentance, so that his prayer and praise not be despised — and although we say "return us," "forgive us," of necessity an arousal from below is needed, as it is said (Malachi 3:7), "return to Me, and I will return to you."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:22: With this one may understand what our sages, of blessed memory, said in Midrash Eichah on the verse (Lamentations 5:21), "turn us back to You, O Lord, and we shall return," in these words: the Assembly of Israel said before the Holy One, blessed be He, Master of the universe, it is Yours to turn us back. He said to them, it is yours, as it is said, "return to Me, and I will return to you." She said before Him, Master of the universe, it is Yours, as it is said (Psalms 85:5), "turn us back, O God of our salvation." Therefore it says, "turn us back to You, O Lord, and we shall return." — end of quotation. The meaning is that Israel ask that the Holy One, blessed be He, open for them the beginnings of repentant thoughts, in the manner of the herald proclaiming that repentant thoughts are coming, and the Holy One, blessed be He, answers that repentance is needed in deed, that they begin with it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:23: In this manner our sages, of blessed memory, said in Midrash Shir HaShirim (Rabbah 5:3): Rabbi Yosi said, [regarding] (Song of Songs 5:2), "open for me, my sister, my love" — the Holy One, blessed be He, said, open for Me an opening the size of the eye of a needle, and I will open for you gates through which wagons and carriages can enter. Rabbi Chanina asked Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, what is the meaning of (Psalms 65:6), "the trust of all the ends of the earth and of the distant seas"? He said to him, repentance is likened to the sea — just as this sea is always open, so the gates of repentance are always open. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:24: A further, fourth exhortation — when a person sees the sudden death of the living, as it is said (Job 34:20), "in a moment they die," etc., and he does not know when he will be called to judgment and reckoning, it is fitting that he rise and hasten to prepare provisions for his journey, for no person is assured of life even for a single day, as they said (Avot 2:10), "repent one day before your death," and they said (Shabbat 153a), "repent today, lest you die tomorrow" — and thus all his days are found in repentance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:25: We find a great rebuke on this matter in Avot (1:14), in the Mishnah, "if I am not for myself, who is for me? And if not now, when?" And the pious Rabbi Yosef Yavetz, peace be upon him, explained, in these words: regarding the intent of the Mishnah, it taught three great matters that guide a person to the place of his completeness. The first: just as a person's life depends on the person himself and not on another — for who else will eat and who else will feel [hunger] for him besides himself — so it is with the life of the soul: if he does not concern himself for his soul, not to corrupt it, who will have mercy on it? Therefore, one who does not learn is deserving of death — for he is deserving of death for having subjugated his glorious soul beneath the feet of his animal soul, and for not having had compassion on it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:26: The second: they already said it is forbidden to travel together with an ignorant person on the road, lest he kill him, and gave the reason: one who has no regard for his own life certainly has none for his fellow's life. Regarding this it says, "if I am not for myself, who is for me?" And even so, perhaps [it is still lacking] — this is what it says, "and when I am for myself, what am I?" — indicating that he should always thirst for Torah and never be satisfied with it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:27: The third: that he not lose a single moment of his time, for when will this moment you are now in come again — not even one just like it — for whoever comes first merits and receives a blessing; one who goes to distant seas to hunt game to bring back, and finds a fitting time for his pursuit, shall he defer it? If this is so regarding the life of the mortal body, how much more so regarding the life of the soul! Or he might say, behold, I am obligated to serve God, blessed be He, all my days, and when shall I complete what I now lack — for it is not fitting to boast of tomorrow, for would that he could stand on his own and pay off what he owes; and so Pharaoh said to Israel (Exodus 5:13), "complete your work, each day's task in its day," and do not boast of tomorrow, for who permitted this to you — are you not obligated to do tomorrow just as much as today? If so, when will you fill the deficiency? This delightful explanation I have gleaned from the words of Rabbi Yehudah ibn Shoshan, of blessed memory. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:28: So too David the king, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 144:4), "man is like a breath, his days are like a passing shadow." And our sages, of blessed memory, said: Solomon said (Ecclesiastes 6:12), "for who knows what is good for man," etc., "like a shadow" — but did not specify which; David his father explained, "his days are like a passing shadow" — if you say like the shadow of a wall, there is substance to it; the shadow of a palm tree, there is substance to it. Which shadow then? Rav Huna said in the name of Rabbi Acha: like the shadow of a bird, which passes and its shadow passes; and Shmuel said, like the shadow of a bee, which has no substance at all. — end of quotation.
